children: Generac Holdings

shares rose as much as 3.1% to a three-month high Thursday after analysts at KeyBanc Capital Markets and Piper Sandler issued bullish reports on the backup-power equipment maker, citing growing demand from artificial intelligence data centers and an opportunity for investors to benefit from a shift in its business.
KeyBanc analyst Jeffrey Hammond upgraded Generac

to Overweight from Sector Weight and established a $280 price target following meetings with Chief Executive Officer Aaron Jagdfeld. Piper Sandler analyst Dimple Gosai initiated coverage with an Overweight rating and a higher $303 target, suggesting roughly 39% upside from Wednesday's reference price of $221.34.
Both analysts said investors are undervaluing Generac's

emerging role as a supplier of backup generators to large data centers. Their arguments differ, however, in the degree of emphasis they place on the company's ability to fulfill existing orders, the potential size of the market and the long-term outlook for its traditional residential business.
Amazon agreement changes investment case
Hammond said Generac's
recently announced agreement to supply Amazon
with as much as $8 billion of generators over seven years provides important evidence that the company can compete with established industrial suppliers.
Following discussions with management, Hammond expressed greater confidence in Generac's
ability to expand production and meet demand from Amazon and other large technology customers.

The agreement includes $2.4 billion in purchases through 2028, with provisions requiring Amazon to pay for at least half of certain committed volumes. Generac expects the Amazon relationship to generate approximately $1.6 billion in revenue in 2028, contributing to management's projection of $3 billion to $3.2 billion in total data center sales that year.

Hammond said the central question for investors has shifted from whether customers want Generac's equipment to whether the company can manufacture enough of it. He cited management's confidence in its engine supplier, Baudouin/Weichai, and its ability to increase production of engines, alternators and cooling systems.

Gosai agreed that the Amazon contract strengthens Generac's competitive position but argued that investors are overlooking a much larger opportunity.She estimated the annual U.S. market for data center backup generators could reach $16 billion to $21 billion through 2032, based on projected growth in computing infrastructure. Her analysis suggests the global market could approach $25 billion annually, exceeding Generac management's earlier estimate of $14 billion to $17 billion.

Gosai also pointed to Generac's roughly $4 billion data center backlog, accumulated in less than a year, as evidence that the business could generate recurring orders rather than a temporary surge in revenue.
Different views on valuation, competition
The analysts share the view that Generac's stock does not fully reflect its transformation from a predominantly residential generator manufacturer into a significant industrial power supplier.

Hammond estimated that Generac trades at approximately 10.8 times his projected 2027 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, below the company's historical valuation range of 12 to 20 times. His $280 target implies a multiple of 13.4 times projected earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or ebitda.
Gosai took a more expansive approach, arguing that investors are valuing Generac primarily as a residential equipment company despite its growing industrial exposure.
She calculated that the shares trade at 9.3 times consensus 2028 ebitda, compared with 9.9 times for residential peers and 15.3 times for commercial and industrial equipment manufacturers.

Her scenario analysis suggests Generac could be worth approximately $334 a share if it captures 17% of the U.S. data center backup-power market. A more optimistic scenario involving a 20% market share produces an estimated value of $407, although that would require additional manufacturing capacity.

Gosai also argued that Generac benefits from production constraints at established competitors such as Caterpillar, Cummins and Rolls-Royce. With some competitors quoting delivery times of 70 to 80 weeks or longer, compared with approximately 40 to 45 weeks for Generac, she expects customers to prioritize availability and reliability over price.

However, she cautioned that Generac is unlikely to match the profitability of larger rivals because it purchases engines rather than manufacturing them internally. Its business also lacks the same proportion of lucrative aftermarket service revenue.
Residential business offers stability
The analysts also offered different perspectives on Generac's residential generator business, which has historically depended on consumer concerns about power outages.

Hammond said residential standby generator demand appears to have stabilized near a cyclical low despite relatively mild storm activity. Sales have remained geographically diverse, suggesting that the business may be less vulnerable to the absence of major hurricanes than investors fear.

He also praised management's increasingly disciplined approach to capital allocation, including several recent divestitures and plans to discontinue or sell clean-energy products unlikely to become profitable by 2027.
Gosai focused more heavily on the demographic forces supporting residential demand over the longer term.

She noted that approximately 65% of Generac's residential standby customers are at least 60 years old. With the U.S. population aging and older households controlling substantial wealth, she expects the potential customer base to expand.
Gosai also estimated that only 6.75% of the roughly 63 million addressable U.S. homes currently have standby generators, leaving considerable room for adoption.

Importantly, she projected that residential operations will decline from approximately 75% of Generac's ebitda in 2025 to about 50% by 2030 as industrial sales grow. That shift could make the company's overall earnings less dependent on unpredictable weather patterns.
Analysts agree on growth but highlight execution risks
Both firms expect substantial earnings growth, although Piper Sandler's projections are somewhat more aggressive.

Hammond raised his 2027 adjusted earnings estimate to $13.90 a share from $11.88 while maintaining his 2026 estimate at $9.85. He now forecasts approximately $1.32 billion in adjusted ebitda for 2027.
Gosai projected approximately $7.09 billion in revenue and $1.42 billion in adjusted EBITDA for 2027, compared with KeyBanc's estimates of approximately $6.68 billion and $1.32 billion, respectively.

The analysts identified manufacturing expansion as a principal risk. Gosai additionally highlighted Generac's reliance on a Chinese-owned engine supplier, potential regulatory changes affecting that relationship, customer concentration among major technology companies and the possibility of slower data center capital spending.

Her report also identified 2029 as a potential test of the investment thesis, when currently committed orders begin to run off and competing manufacturers are expected to have expanded their own production capacity.

For investors, the two reports suggest that Generac's valuation increasingly depends on whether it can convert its data center backlog into sustained revenue and profit growth. Hammond sees the Amazon agreement and management's execution plans as sufficient justification for an upgrade, while Gosai argues that the market has yet to appreciate the company's potential share of a rapidly expanding industry.

Both see substantial upside, but their forecasts leave investors with a question that will become increasingly important as Generac expands production: whether today's surge in demand represents the foundation of a lasting industrial power business or a particularly profitable phase of the AI infrastructure construction boom.

title: Generac shares rise to 3-mth high as KeyBanc, Piper Sandler see data center growth
